title: Middle East dust as an important external driver of the Indian Ocean Dipole

paper_content.abstract: The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) strongly influences Indo-Pacific climate extremes, yet its drivers remain incompletely understood. Using satellite observations, reanalysis, and climate model experiments, we identify Middle East dust emissions as a major external driver of IOD variability. Observational evidence shows that dust over the 1980-2020 period account for ~36% of interannual IOD variance, surpassing El Niño-Southern Oscillation as the main driver during boreal autumn. Climate simulations confirm that reduced dust enhances warming in the western Indian Ocean and induce easterly winds that shoal the eastern thermocline. These anomalies trigger Bjerknes and wind–evaporation–sea surface temperature feedbacks, amplifying a positive IOD pattern, and vice versa. Our findings reveal a powerful dust–IOD teleconnection, highlighting the need to incorporate aerosol forcing into seasonal forecasts and climate projections.
paper_content.introduction:
The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) is the major mode of interannual climate variability in the Tropical Indian Ocean (TIO), marked by a seesaw pattern of sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies between the western and eastern TIO1,2. This anomalous SST pattern leads to changes in atmospheric circulation and rainfall patterns over the vast areas surrounding TIO, including Indonesia, India, Australia, and East Africa3–5. Positive IOD (pIOD) events bring warming to the western basin and cooling to the east, reshaping rainfall patterns across East Africa, India, Indonesia, and Australia, while negative phases (nIOD) have opposite effects. The extreme pIOD event in 2019 triggered unprecedented Australian bushfires and historic flooding along the Yangtze River6–8, underscoring the urgent need to understand the mechanism underlying IOD events. Most studies attribute IOD variability to external forcing4,9, internal air–sea interactions and remote El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) influences1,10,11, yet the role of aerosols remains largely unexplored. The TIO is located close to the world’s second largest dust source—the Middle East deserts. Previous studies have identified the far-reaching impacts of Middle East dust on the South Asian monsoon, Arabian Sea SST, and Indian summer monsoon rainfall12–14. Around 2010, both IOD behavior and Middle East dust emissions shifted markedly, with IOD transitioning from frequent negative to positive phases and Middle East dust emissions reaching historically low levels by 201915–18. This coincidence motivates our investigation into whether dust forcing influences IOD phases and quantifies its contribution to the variability of IOD.

Here, we show that variability in summertime Middle East dust (SMED) is a critical driver of autumn IOD events. Using model experiments, we establish a causal link where reduced SMED triggers a chain of atmosphere-ocean interactions in the tropical Indian Ocean. These interactions, primarily driven by wind-induced ocean dynamics and reinforced by cloud feedbacks, robustly promote the development of positive IOD conditions.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Liu et al. estimated that dust aerosols from the Middle East regions act as a dominant external driver of the Indian Ocean Dipole. In particular, they show that summertime dust over the 1980-2020 period accounts for ~36% of interannual IOD variance, surpassing the El Niño-Southern Oscillation as the main driver during boreal autumn, using satellite observations and reanalysis. In addition, they perform CSEM v1.2 with the Parallel Ocean Program (POP2) and Community Atmosphere Model simulations (CAMS 4.3) to show that reduced summertime Middle East dust enhances warming in the western Indian Ocean during boreal autumn and induces easterly winds that shoal the eastern thermocline. This tilts of the thermocline, deepening it in the west and shoaling it in the east, and reinforces the SST gradient through the Bjerknes and wind–evaporation–sea surface temperature (WES) feedback, amplifying a positive IOD pattern, and vice versa.
Overall, the central findings are scientifically interesting and clearly relevant to Indian Ocean climate variability, particularly the assessment that summertime Middle East dust explains a large fraction of IOD interannual variance, potentially surpassing ENSO’s influence during boreal autumn. However, characterizing Middle Eastern dust aerosols as the dominant external driver of IOD variability is currently overstated. A more explicit differentiation between the impacts of Middle Eastern dust and those of Central and East Asian dust emissions is required, as both may modulate the IOD. Furthermore, additional forcings and modes of variability, including anthropogenic aerosols, greenhouse gases, the Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO), and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), can also affect IOD variability during boreal autumn. These contributions should be carefully separated and quantified before making the strong claim that Middle East dust is the dominant external driver of the IOD.
Dust variability can both drive and respond to IOD variability. However, this bidirectional relationship does not yet appear to be well constrained in the authors’ analysis of dust–IOD interactions, partly because of substantial uncertainty in the representation of dust emissions in the global climate model CESM v1.2 (Kok et al., 2022; main text reference 18). Given this known bias, the authors should more clearly justify their choice of CESM v1.2 with CAMS 4.3 for this study and explain how this underestimate might affect their conclusions regarding dust–IOD interactions.
Prior work has linked anthropogenic aerosols and greenhouse gases to Indian Ocean warming and IOD-like patterns, and has also shown that Middle East and West Asian dust influences the South Asian monsoon and Arabian Sea SST (see Banerjee and Kumar, 2016; Jin et al., 2014; Zheng and Hoteit, 2025). Also, It has been shown that Indian summer monsoon rainfall responds positively to Middle East dust (Jin and Yang, 2014). These findings from previous studies should be discussed explicitly in the main manuscript.

-Jin, Qinjian, Jiangfeng Wei, and Zong‐Liang Yang. "Positive response of Indian summer rainfall to Middle East dust." Geophysical Research Letters 41, no. 11 (2014): 4068-4074.
-Zheng, Yiling, and Ibrahim Hoteit. "Asymmetric impacts of Indian Ocean Dipole on summer climate over Arabian Peninsula." Geophysical Research Letters 52, no. 20 (2025): e2025GL118195.
General comments:
-Please use other reanalysis datasets (e.g., ERA5-CAMS, NAAPS) and satellite dust AOD products to check if the observed dust AOD pattern variability is reliable. In particular, since MODIS DOD has known bias, please cross-validate with IASI-DAOD or other independent datasets (such as CALIPSO).
-Line #72: MISR only provides aerosol data from approximately year 2000 onward, whereas the caption of Fig. 1 states the MISR non-spherical aerosol optical depth data from 1980 to 2023. This should be corrected. If other datasets are combined for the pre-MISR period, this should be clearly mentioned in the figure caption.
-In Fig. 1a, it is not clear whether the regression is performed on climatological means or on individual years. I assume the regression is currently done for individual years, comparing dust during JJA with other meteorological values during SON.
-The rationale for using different time periods for the datasets is unclear, such as most satellite dust DOD cover 2003–2023, while dust station data spans 1980–2023. The manuscript should clarify the reason and discuss any resulting limitations and uncertainties in the analysis.
Lines 117-120: “Reduced Middle East dust emissions are statistically linked to atmospheric and oceanic states resembling pIOD events, suggesting that decadal variations in dust loading likely exert an important, previously underappreciated influence on tropical Indian Ocean climate.” It is not clear whether the authors remove ENSO-related variability from SST fields (in Fig. 1 and Extended Figs 1–5) before computing the IOD index. Also, there are several confounding factors that can also influence the IOD, such as the MJO and the PDO. The manuscript should detail how these confounding factors are accounted for or removed in the dust–IOD statistical analyses. Please cite that previous work here, especially when stated as “previously underappreciated influence on tropical Indian Ocean climate.”
Lines #31-35: The use of summertime station-based dust-frequency observations to scale annual-mean dust mass density in CESM v1.2 needs further justification. Could you please clarify why the other seasons were not considered? This could potentially underestimate the true annual mean dust mass density. The authors should also clarify this methodological choice and its possible implications.
Line # 142- “Both the spatial configuration and the intensity of these anomalies strongly indicate that SMED acts as an external forcing capable of generating pronounced interannual variability in the TIO”. This conclusion is currently overstated, as the authors are not investigating the impact of other aerosols on IOD changes. How do PDO and MJO manifest in changes in IOD, since they are also affected by dust forcing, which in turn can affect the positive and negative phases of IOD?
Lines # 57-60, Supplementary Information (extended Fig. S6). Why, in the extended Fig. 6a, are they not including the SMED versus DMI sim? It would be good to plot the correlation coefficient and also the SVD analysis for this simulation run. As shown in Fig. S6b, the observations are quite off for the SMED and DMI patterns from 2010 onwards. What could be the reason for that?
Line 474: Please cite the methodology and relevant references related to the implementation of Singular Value Decomposition Analysis.
Lines #212-215; “Once transported, these aerosols exert a strong radiative forcing by absorbing solar radiation, which heats the upper troposphere, while simultaneously reducing the amount of shortwave radiation reaching the ocean surface”.
-It depends on the dust mineralogy as well; without constraining that over SMED, it is perhaps uncertain to quantify that. Authors should also consider providing the heating rate map rather than showing changes in surface radiative flux. That is important for assessing how much the radiative heating rate changes. To correctly determine vertical radiative heating rates, authors could consider the vertical profiles of dust extinction. Authors should also use the CALIPSO data or the CESM-based vertical profile of the dust extinctions to identify changes in heating rates.
-Please explain why the TIO low cloud fraction is decreasing, and the high cloud fraction is increasing in the reduced-dust over SMED scenarios. How are authors constraining the other aerosols in the CESM v1.2 setup? Are authors only changing dust aerosol, or are they also changing other aerosols, such as sea salt aerosol in CESM v1.2 setup?
Lines #225-227 “These changes significantly affect cloud dynamics, driving a decrease in low-level cloud cover and an increase in high-level clouds over the western TIO (Fig. 3c, d).” Figure S8 and Figure 3 show otherwise. I see an enhanced low cloud fraction from the CSEM runs over the Western TIO. Please explain.
Lines #227-230: This needed a detailed investigation of the cloud feedback; the authors should cite past work for this statement here: “The transformation of cloud fields further modifies the radiative budget by increasing both longwave and shortwave radiation, thereby amplifying the warming signal over the western TIO in synergy with the direct radiative effects of reduced dust.”
Lines 232-237: Did the authors run the CESM v1.2 simulation from 1980 to 2020, or from 2010 to 2020?
Line 288 and other places: “Furthermore, analysis of the month-to-month evolution of the IOD signal (figures omitted)”. The figure not shown does not look ideal. Please consider including all referenced figures in the supplementary materials.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The manuscript investigates the role of mineral dust aerosols from the Middle East in modulating interannual variability of the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD). Using a combination of satellite observations, reanalysis datasets, and climate model experiments, the authors demonstrate that variations in summer dust emissions between 1980 and 2020 explain approximately 36% of the observed interannual IOD variance—exceeding the influence of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) during boreal autumn. Overall, the paper identifies a previously underappreciated dust–IOD teleconnection, emphasizing the importance of aerosol forcing in seasonal prediction and long-term climate projections. Overall, the work is novel, and supported by comprehensive analysis. However, the manuscript is not always easy to follow, as several figure captions and axis labels lack clarity and may cause confusion for readers. I recommend publication after revision to address the points detailed below.
Major comments:
1. The paper explains how dust emission reduction over Middle East causes a positive anomaly in solar radiation reaching to the western Indian ocean surface. However, it does not clearly discuss how this enhanced radiative energy translates into a positive SST anomaly, considering the ocean’s large heat capacity. Please expand on this physical mechanism. Is the ~2-month lag used in the analysis related to the ocean mixed-layer adjustment timescale?
2. Please explain why there is a positive net LW flux at surface over the western Indian ocean in the case of dust deduction? Moreover, for both SW and LW, why the flux anomaly over eastern Indian ocean is always opposite to the western part?
Specific comments:
3. Line 88, ‘reversing the regression coefficients to represent dust reduction’ is very confusing, I figured out its meaning when I looked at the figure caption of Fig. S3, it means you take the negative values of the regression coefficient. Please modify the sentence, and also clarify it in the caption of Fig.1.
4. Fig S3, you mentioned ‘regression coefficient’ and ‘correlation coefficient’ in the figure caption, are they the same? Please clarify what you used and keep them consistent.
5. In Fig1 (e), please clarify that the grey dashed line is the mixed layer depth anomaly, right? It is not just mixed layer depth. Also, please clarify the grey dashed line is corresponding to the y-axis on the right. Otherwise, it’s too confusing.
6. Line 93, ‘0.5K per standard deviation of dust variability’, please clarify the meaning of this term. Authors use different dust proxies, e.g., dust AOD, column mass density, and dust frequency, what are their standard deviation of dust variability, respectively.
7. Line 336, ‘suppress eastern upwelling’, should that be suppress eastern downwelling?

emissions and IOD phases, and that future studies using targeted numerical

variability, reinforced by sensitivity experiments that seek to isolate the dust influence

Reply: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We have revised the manuscript to
provide a more detailed mechanistic explanation of the cloud feedback, supported by
key literature.
The text now explicitly states that the increase in shortwave radiation results from
reduced low-level clouds (e.g., stratocumulus), which decreases planetary albedo.
Conversely, the increase in longwave radiation is linked to enhanced high-level cloud
cover (e.g., cirrus), which amplifies thegreenhouse effect.
This explanation is now grounded in established cloud-radiative feedback theory,
supported by previous studies. The revised text presents a logically supported process
rather than an assertion.
Wealso cited therevised texthere forconvenience.
The transformation of cloud fields—characterized by a reduction in low-level cloud
fraction and an increase in high-level cloud fraction—further modifies the radiative
budget (Figs. 3a, b). Specifically, the decrease in low clouds reduces the albedo,
allowing more shortwave radiation to penetrate and warm the ocean surface 37,38.
Concurrently, the increase in high clouds enhances the atmospheric greenhouse effect
by absorbing and re-emitting longwave radiation, which inhibits radiative cooling at
the surface 37,39. These two effects act in synergy with the direct radiative effect of
reduced dust loading to amplify the warming signal over the western TIO. This cloud
feedback process, particularly the low-cloud albedo feedback, is well-established as a
key positivefeedback mechanism modulating TIOvariability.

This study examined how mineral dust aerosols emitted from the Middle East a7ect
the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) using both observational data and the CESM model.
While previous studies have examined how anthropogenic aerosols effect IOD, how
Middle Eastern dust aerosols affect the IOD is largely unclear. The study addresses a

overall analysis is quite comprehensive, however, some details in model setting, the

subsequently trigger an IOD event in the following season through air–sea

3. The radiative forcing of the dust aerosols are shown in both the coupled CESM
simulations and atmosphere-only model (CAM) runs. However, the location of
radiative forcing directly from the dust aerosols. With reduced Middle Eastern dust
aerosols, one would expect to see enhanced shortwave (SW) fluxes (i.e., warming)

However, this pattern is not clearly shown in the coupled simulation (Fig. S8c)--there

Reply: Thank you for this insightful observation regarding the spatial pattern of
surface shortwave radiation response in our coupled model experiments. You have
correctly identified a key nuance in how dust aerosol impacts manifest in coupled
versus atmosphere-only simulations.
You rightly noted that reduced Middle Eastern dust should directly enhance surface
shortwave fluxes over dust-laden regions from the Arabian Peninsula to the Arabian
Sea. This expected response is clearly present in our atmosphere-only (CAM)
experiments, as shown in Extended Data Fig. 14a.The different pattern in the coupled
(CESM) simulation—with cooling near 12°N and warming displaced farther
south—is indeed attributable to ocean-atmosphere coupling and the associated
teleconnections as you suggested. The initial radiative perturbation triggers a specific
chain of adjustments:
(1) Circulation Adjustment: The surface warming over the western Tropical Indian
Ocean (TIO) enhances convection and establishes a low-pressure anomaly (Fig. 2c).
This sets up a basin-scale pressure gradient, driving an anomalous clockwise vertical
circulation and generating prevailing anomalous easterly winds at the surface over the
centralTIO, oppositetotheclimatological westerlies (Fig. 2c-d).
(2) Mechanism for the Displaced Warming: These easterly anomalies suppress the
eastward advection of warm water and, through Bjerknes and wind-evaporation-SST
(WES) feedbacks, help sustain and confine the core of the warming signal further
south, near 6°N–6°S.
(3) Mechanism for the Cooling near 12°N: Crucially, in the region near 12°N
(Arabian Sea), the circulation adjustment leads to a strengthening of the prevailing
climatological winds (Fig. 2c, vectors). This increase in surface wind speed enhances
local evaporation, which produces a net surface cooling via the WES feedback. This
wind-driven cooling effectively counteracts and overshadows the direct radiative
warming from dust reduction, resulting in the net cooling anomaly observed in
Extended Data Fig. 14c.
In summary, the coupling-induced atmospheric circulation adjustment—particularly
the wind speed changes and the subsequent WES feedback—redistributes the thermal
response, explaining both the southward shift of the warming and the localized
cooling around 12°N.
Therefore, we have expanded the discussion in the revised manuscript to explicitly
address thismechanism.Wealso cited thediscussion here for convenience.
Moreover, the atmospheric-only simulation exhibits a radiative response that is
spatially coherent with the dust aerosol distribution (Extended Data Fig. 14), while
the coupled simulation displays additional spatial heterogeneity due to oceanic
adjustments (Extended Data Fig. 11). This redistribution likely stems from
ocean-atmosphere coupling, wherein the initial radiative perturbation triggers
atmospheric circulation adjustments andsubsequent wind-evaporation-SSTfeedbacks,
creating secondary radiative perturbations that partially obscure the direct
dust–radiation signal, which is ultimately manifested as a teleconnected response.
Nevertheless, both experiments consistently support the proposed physical framework
linkingMiddle Eastern dust forcing to IODvariability.
4. In the CAM simulations, enhanced SW fluxes do appear from southern Arabian
Peninsula towards the Arabian Sea (Figs. S13a, S10a), but mainly over the northern

Reply: Thank you for this perceptive question, which gets to the heart of the
dynamical mechanisms at play. You are correct in observing that the enhanced SW
fluxes in the CAM simulations are concentrated over the northern and easternArabian
Sea, with a weaker direct signal over the western tropical Indian Ocean. This spatial
structure indeed implies that the local radiative forcing from reduced dust does not
remain confined, but rather initiates an atmospheric teleconnection that propagates its
influence downstream.
Themechanism isa three-step process:
(1) Local Radiative Forcing & Atmospheric Adjustment: Reduced dust over the
Arabian Peninsula/northern Arabian Sea increases surface SW absorption, creating a
strong vertical heating gradient (surface warming, relative upper-level cooling;
Extended Data Figs.11, 13a).Thismodifies local stabilityand circulation.
(2) Atmospheric Teleconnection & Downstream Cloud Response: The adjusted
circulation and zonal cell (Fig. 2d) act as a teleconnection bridge, transporting the
perturbation's influence to the western TIO. This alters the vertical thermodynamic
profile, driving a characteristic cloud reorganization there: decreased low-level and
increased high-level cloud cover (Fig. 3c, d). In the atmosphere-only (CAM) run, this
teleconnected response is constrained by fixed SSTs, explaining the weaker direct
maritimesignal.
(3) Amplification via Ocean-Atmosphere Coupling: This step explains the stronger
oceanic signal in the coupled model. The teleconnected cloud changes (Step 2) now
interact with the ocean. Reduced low cloud cover increases surface shortwave
radiation, leading to SST warming. This warming then activates powerful positive
feedback loops: the cloud–SST feedback further suppressing low clouds (Lin et al.,
2025; Wu et al., 2025; Wyant et al., 1997), the Bjerknes feedback and the
wind‑evaporation‑SST (WES) feedback. These coupled feedbacks dramatically
amplify and extend theinitial atmospheric perturbation.
Therefore, the CAM pattern confirms the dust reduction initiates an atmospheric
teleconnection. The coupling with the ocean is essential to transform this initial
adjustment into the stronger, basin-scale ocean-atmosphere feedbacks that effectively
drive the IOD development, as detailed in our manuscript. We have expanded the
discussion in the revised manuscript to explicitly address this mechanism. We also
cited thediscussion here for convenience.
Notably, the spatial pattern of the SW flux response in the CAM simulations, with its
maximum over the northern and eastern Arabian Sea rather than uniformly across the
basin (Extended Data Fig. 17a &c), suggests that the radiative impact of dust
reduction initiates an atmospheric teleconnection. The initial perturbation mainly
over the land likely alters regional atmospheric heating and circulation patterns 46-48,
which in turn redistributes the energy downstream, setting the stage for the more
extensive and evident ocean-atmosphere signals and feedbacks that propagating to
theTIOin thecoupled model.

Reply: We thank you for raising these important questions regarding our model
configuration, which we are pleased to clarify. In our CESM1.2 coupled simulations,
only the emissions of dust aerosols were modified between the control and sensitivity
experiments. All other external forcings, including anthropogenic aerosols (e.g.,
sulfate, black carbon, organic carbon) and greenhouse gases, were included in the
model and prescribed at their default, present-day levels. These non-dust forcings
were held constant throughout the 1980–2020 simulation period and did not vary
interannually.
The coupled model was initialized from a pre-industrial control run and subsequently
spun up for five years prior to the beginning of our formal experimental period (1980)
(Xie et al., 2018). This spin-up duration ensured that the model's ocean and
atmosphere components reached astableequilibrium under theprescribed forcing.
We have added a detailed description of the experimental design, including the
aerosol and greenhouse gas forcing specifications and the spin-up procedure to the
revised manuscript for greater clarity.
To isolate the impact of Middle Eastern dust (10° S–30° N, 35° E–70° E) on
interannual IOD variability, we drove CESM with observed summertime dust mixing
ratio over the Middle East for 1980–2020 and diagnosed the resulting IOD index.
Specifically, the summertime-mean dust loading in CESM was rescaled each year
using the region’s summertime station dust frequency observations, generating a
transient dust-mass time series that faithfully captures observed variability. Other
aerosols were prescribed at their default, present-day levels and not altered in the
sensitivity simulations. Five ensemble members—generated by perturbing initial
temperature fields over land and ocean—were averaged to suppress internal climate
noise. The magnitude of the temperature perturbation is 1×10-14 K 93. The coupled
model was also initialized from a pre-industrial control run and subsequently spun up
for five years under present-day forcing conditions prior to the beginning of our
formal experimental period (1980). This spin-up duration ensured the model's ocean
and atmosphere components reached a stable equilibrium under the prescribed
forcing 94. All atmospheric variables and the IOD index were then regressed onto
regionaldust loadingto quantifythedust-driven changes from1980to 2020.

12. Line 158, this seems to contradict the statement in lines 134-135. Could you
please clarify what thesystematicbiases are?
Reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment, which highlights
a need for greater clarity in our discussion. The two statements address
complementary rather than contradictory aspects of the model's performance, and we
have revised the text toeliminateany potential formisunderstanding.
The statement in Lines 134-135 emphasizes the model's success in reproducing the
spatial pattern of the dust-IOD relationship—namely, the large-scale dipole structure
over the tropical Indian Ocean. This demonstrates that the fundamental physical
linkage is captured bythemodel.
In contrast, the statement in Line 158 pertains to the attenuation of the temporal
correlation coefficient (i.e., the simulated correlation is systematically lower than
observed). One key reason for this attenuation is the model's inherent systematic
biases in its representation of IOD dynamics. These include well-documented biases
inclimate models, such as an overly strong thermocline feedback in theeastern Indian
Ocean, an exaggerated seasonal cycle, or an inaccurate mean state (Yao et al., 2016;
Xiao et al., 2022). Such biases do not necessarily prevent the model from simulating
the correct spatial pattern of the IOD's SST anomalies, but they can distort the
amplitude and precise timing of its evolution. This distortion in the dynamics
introduces "noise" into the simulated year-to-year relationship between dust (SMED)
and theDipole Mode Index (DMI), thereby collectively amplifying thedeviation from
observations inthestrength of thetemporal correlation.
To clarify this, we have revised the relevant sentence in the manuscript and cited it
here.
Nevertheless, the simulated correlation coefficient remains systematically lower than
that estimated by observation. This attenuation is attributable to (i) the reliance of the
model on station-based dust frequency to scale column-integrated dust-mass density,
which introduces additional sampling uncertainty, and (ii) systematic biases in the
model’s representation of IOD dynamics (e.g., in the thermocline feedback and
seasonal phase locking), which distort the precise evolution of the mode and
collectively amplify the attenuation of the simulated correlation relative to
observations.

15. Line 220, “Increased solar radiation penetrates to the surface…” , this is not

shortwave radiation at the surface in the fully coupled model experiment (Fig. S8c)

because the CESM is a fully coupled climate model. The initial radiative perturbation
from dust reduction triggers a chain of ocean-atmosphere interactions, including
adjustments in atmospheric circulation and wind-evaporation-SST feedbacks. These
processes redistribute the energy downstream, generating secondary radiative
anomalies that can partially mask the direct local signal. This energy redistribution is
a fundamental feature of the coupled climate system and is the key mechanism that
establishes theremote teleconnection pattern wedescribe.
In contrast, as the reviewer might anticipate, a parallel experiment conducted with an
atmosphere-only model (CAM, Extended Data Fig. 14c) does show a clear and
localized increase in net shortwave radiation confined to the dust source region, as it
lacks these ocean-mediated feedbacks. The comparison between these two
experiments robustly demonstrates how the direct radiative forcing from dust evolves
intoa broader teleconnection within acoupled framework.
We have clarified this crucial point in the revised manuscript to better guide the
reader's interpretation ofExtended Data Fig.11c.Wealso cited theclarification here.
Moreover, the atmospheric-only simulation exhibits a radiative response that is
spatially coherent with the dust aerosol distribution (Extended Data Fig. 14), while
the coupled simulation displays additional spatial heterogeneity due to oceanic
adjustments (Extended Data Fig. 11). This redistribution likely stems from
ocean-atmosphere coupling, wherein the initial radiative perturbation triggers
atmospheric circulation adjustments andsubsequent wind-evaporation-SSTfeedbacks,
creating secondary radiative perturbations that partially obscure the direct
dust–radiation signal, which is ultimately manifested as a teleconnected response.

linkingMiddle Eastern dust forcing to IODvariability.

18.Line 267, the response of shortwave fluxes is mainly over the land. How does the
signal propagate to theTIO?
Reply: Thank you for raising this question.The signal propagates from the land tothe
Tropical Indian Ocean (TIO) primarily through an atmospheric teleconnection. The
mechanism is athree-step process:
(1) Local Radiative Forcing & Atmospheric Adjustment: Reduced dust over the
Arabian Peninsula/northern Arabian Sea increases surface SW absorption, creating a
strong vertical heating gradient (surface warming, relative upper-level cooling;
Extended Data Figs.11, 13a).Thismodifies local stabilityand circulation.
(2) Atmospheric Teleconnection & Downstream Cloud Response: The adjusted
circulation and zonal cell (Fig. 2d) act as a teleconnection bridge, transporting the
perturbation's influence to the western TIO. This alters the vertical thermodynamic
profile, driving a characteristic cloud reorganization there: decreased low-level and
increased high-level cloud cover (Fig. 3c, d). In the atmosphere-only (CAM) run, this
teleconnected response is limited by fixed SSTs, explaining the weaker direct
maritimesignal.
(3) Amplification via Ocean-Atmosphere Coupling: This step explains the stronger
oceanic signal in the coupled model. The teleconnected cloud changes (Step 2) now
interact with the ocean. Reduced low clouds enhance surface SW, warming the SST.
This warming then triggers powerful positive feedbacks: the cloud–SST feedback
further suppressing low clouds (Lin et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Wyant et al., 1997),
the Bjerknes feedbacks and wind-evaporation-SST (WES) feedbacks. These coupled
feedbacks dramatically amplify and extend theinitial atmosphericperturbation.
Therefore, the CAM pattern confirms the dust reduction initiates an atmospheric
teleconnection. The coupling with the ocean is essential to transform this initial
adjustment into the stronger, basin-scale ocean-atmosphere feedbacks that effectively
drivetheIOD development, as detailed inourmanuscript.
In summary, the dust-induced radiative heating over the Middle East perturbs the
regional atmospheric circulation, which in turn triggers a remote response that
influences theTIO.
We have systematically elaborated this dynamical pathway in the revised manuscript
within the " Mechanism: how dust shapes the IOD" section, detailing the key
processes of (1) local radiative adjustment, (2) atmospheric bridge via zonal cell
circulation, and (3) amplification through air-sea feedbacks, and we refer the reader to
that discussionhere.
We have also clarified this dynamical pathway in the revised manuscript and cited it
here.
The initial perturbation mainly over the land likely alters regional atmospheric
heating and circulation patterns 46-48, which in turn redistributes the energy
downstream, setting the stage for the more extensive and evident ocean-atmosphere
signalsandfeedbacks that propagating to theTIOinthe coupled model.

Summary:
The manuscript investigates the role of mineral dust aerosols from the Middle East in
modulating interannual variability of the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD). Using a
combination of satellite observations, reanalysis datasets, and climate model
experiments, the authors demonstrate that variations in summer dust emissions
between 1980 and 2020 explain approximately 36% of the observed interannual IOD
variance—exceeding the influence of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO)
during boreal autumn. Overall, the paper identifies a previously underappreciated
dust–IOD teleconnection, emphasizing the importance of aerosol forcing in seasonal
prediction and long-term climate projections. Overall, the work is novel, and
supported by comprehensive analysis. However, the manuscript is not always easy to
follow, as several figure captions and axis labels lack clarity and may cause confusion
for readers. I recommend publication after revision to address the points detailed
below.
Reply: We are grateful to the reviewer for his/her insightful and very valuable
suggestions, which have significantly contributed to the enhancement of our
manuscript. We have carefully addressed the comments and made the necessary
revisions, hoping that the updated version meets the journal's standards. Our
responses to each of the comments and suggestions are as follows. The referee’s
original comments are shown in blue. Our replies are shown in black. The
corresponding changes in themanuscript are shown in Italicblack.
1. The paper explains how dust emission reduction over Middle East causes a
positive anomaly in solar radiation reaching to the western Indian ocean surface.
However, it does not clearly discuss how this enhanced radiative energy translates
into a positive SST anomaly, considering the ocean’s large heat capacity. Please
expand on this physical mechanism. Is the ~2-month lag used in the analysis related
tothe ocean mixed-layer adjustment timescale?
Reply: We thank the reviewer for raising this crucial point regarding the mechanism
linking enhanced solar radiation to the positive SST anomaly. We agree that a clearer
discussion of this process is essential and have expanded upon it in the revised
manuscript.
The translation of increased net surface shortwave radiation into a positive SST
anomaly occurs through the gradual heat accumulation withinthe ocean's mixed layer.
The ~2-month lag used in our analysis is indeed closely related to the mixed-layer
adjustment timescale for the western Indian Ocean. Case studies in the tropical Indian
Ocean have shown that the thermodynamic response of the mixed layer to sustained
atmospheric forcing (such as radiative anomalies) can manifest over a period of
approximately2to 2.5months (Azaneu, 2022).
In our case, the persistent positive anomaly in net surface heat flux (dominated by
shortwave radiation) progressively heats the relatively shallow mixed layer typical of
the western tropical Indian Ocean. The observed lag represents the integrated time
required for this accumulated heat to become a robust SST signal, consistent with the
established mixed-layer response timescale for this region. We have incorporated this
explanationwith supporting references into therevised discussion section.
Thetranslation of increased shortwave radiation into the initial SSTanomaly involves
thegradual heat accumulation withinthe ocean's mixed layer.Theobserved ~2-month
lag reflects the mixed-layer adjustment timescale, which is approximately 2 to 2.5
months for sustained thermal forcing in the TIO 34. Given the relatively shallow mixed
layer in the western Indian Ocean 35-37, this persistent radiative forcing can efficiently
warm the upper ocean within this timeframe, overcoming the damping from mixing
andlatentheat loss.
2. Please explain why there is a positive net LW flux at surface over the western
Indian ocean in the case of dust deduction? Moreover, for both SW and LW, why the
flux anomaly over eastern Indian ocean isalways oppositeto thewestern part?
Reply: We thank the reviewer for these insightful questions regarding the surface
energy balance.
(1) Positive net LW flux anomaly over the western Indian Ocean: The positive
anomaly in net surface longwave (LW) radiation is a result of coupled atmospheric
adjustments. We propose two complementary mechanisms:First, as previously noted,
the initial warming and enhanced evaporation increase atmospheric water vapor,
which strengthens downward LW radiation. Second, and importantly, the dust
reduction triggers an atmospheric teleconnection that perturbs cloud fields. As
elaborated below, this leads to increased high-level cloudiness over the western IO
basin. These high clouds are highly effective at emitting LW radiation downward,
thereby significantly contributing to the observed positive net LWflux anomaly at the
surface.Wehave also incorporated theexplanation in therevised manuscript andcited
ithere.
The transformation of cloud fields further modifies the radiative budget by increasing
both longwave and shortwave radiation, thereby amplifying the warming signal over
the western TIO in synergy with increased SW and LW radiative fluxes over this
region of reduced dust (Figs. 3a, b). Moreover, the initial warming and enhanced
evaporation might increase atmospheric water vapor over the western TIO, which
strengthensdownwardLWradiation(Fig. 3b).
(2) Dipole pattern of flux anomalies: The opposing flux anomalies are a direct
manifestation of the zonal atmospheric circulation cell excited by the Middle East
dust forcing. Over the western basin, the large-scale ascendance leads to reduced
low-level cloudiness, allowing more shortwave radiation to penetrate to the surface
(positive SW anomaly). Concurrently, the circulation fosters increased high-level
cloudiness, which traps longwave radiation (positive LW anomaly). Over the eastern
basin, the opposite vertical motion and cloud adjustments occur (increased low-cloud
and decreased high-cloud) because of the anomalous zonal circulation, resulting in
negative SW and LW flux anomalies. We have incorporated this physical
interpretation into the revised manuscript to provide a more mechanistic explanation
ofthesurface flux changes and cited ithere.
Moreover, the dipole pattern of radiative flux anomalies over the TIO arises from the
anomalous zonal circulation (Fig. 2d) andzonal asymmetryin cloud vertical structure
(Fig. 3c, d). Over the western basin, diminished low-level clouds enhance incoming
shortwave radiation, while increased high-level clouds trap outgoing longwave
radiation, leading to positive anomalies in both SW and LW fluxes. Conversely, the
eastern basin exhibits opposite cloud adjustments—more low-level and fewer
high-level clouds—resultingin reduced surface radiativefluxes.
3. Line 88, ‘reversing the regression coefficients to represent dust reduction’is very
confusing, I figured out its meaning when I looked at the figure caption of Fig. S3, it
means you take the negative values of the regression coefficient. Please modify the
sentence, andalso clarify it in thecaption of Fig.1.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this lack of clarity. We have modified
the sentence and clarified the caption of Fig. 1 to explicitly state that the patterns for
dust reduction were obtained by taking the negative values of the regression
coefficients.Wealso cited them here forconvenience.
To quantify the dust-IOD connection, we regressed SON SST anomalies over the
tropical Indian Ocean against SMED and took the negative values of the regression
coefficients toindicatedust reduction.
4. Fig S3, you mentioned ‘regression coefficient’and ‘correlation coefficient’in the
figure caption, are they the same? Please clarify what you used and keep them
consistent.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for highlighting this inconsistency. Indeed, the two
terms are different and the analysis presented is based on the regression coefficient.
We have corrected the caption of Fig. S3 (and any other relevant figures) to
consistently use the term "regression coefficient" throughout the manuscript to avoid
any confusion.
5. In Fig1 (e), please clarify that the grey dashed line is the mixed layer depth
anomaly, right? It is not just mixed layer depth. Also, please clarify the grey dashed
lineiscorresponding to they-axis ontheright. Otherwise, it’s too confusing.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. The reviewer is correct. The grey
dashed line in Fig. 1e represents the mixed layer depth anomaly. We have revised the
figure caption to explicitly state this and to clarify that it corresponds to the right
y-axis,in order to eliminateany potential confusion.
Wealso cited it here forconvenience.
Fig. 1. Dust proxies, sea surface temperature and meteorological field regressed on
dust time series. (a) The regression coefficients of JJA station dust record on its
regional mean (averaged over the 10°S~30°N, 35°E~70°E). (b) Similar to a, but for
the JJA MISR non-spherical aerosol optical depth (AOD, also averaged over the
10°S~30°N, 35°E~70°E). (c) Time series of standardized JJA station dust frequency
(the solid line) from 1980 to 2023, and JJA MISR non-spherical aerosol optical depth
(the dashed line) from 2003 to 2023. (d-g) The detrended regression coefficients of
SON meteorological fields on the detrended JJA MISR non-spherical aerosol optical
depth averaged over the Middle East from 2003 to 2023. These meteorological fields
include (d) sea surface temperature. (e) meridional mean (20°S-20°N) vertical cross
section of temperature (shaded) and mixed layer depth anomaly (the gray dashed
line), (f) sea level pressure (shaded) with 850 hPa zonal and meridional wind (UV,
vectors, m/s), and (g) meridional mean (20°S-20°N) vertical cross section of
geopotential height (GPH, shaded) with zonal and vertical wind (UW, vectors, m/s).
These coefficients were scaled by the magnitude of dust decreasing from 2010 to 2020
in the JJA MISR non-spherical aerosol optical depth dataset. The right y-axis in (e)
corresponds to the mixed layer depth; the grey dashed line represents its zero value.
The regression is currently done for individual years. The area with white dots passed
thesignificancetest of p ≤ 0.05byStudent'st-test.
6. Line 93, ‘0.5K per standard deviation of dust variability’, please clarify the
meaning ofthis term.Authors usedifferent dust proxies, e.g., dustAOD, column mass
density, and dust frequency, what are their standard deviation of dust variability,
respectively.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this important clarification. The statement “~0.5 K
per standard deviation of dust variability” should be interpreted as a statistical
estimate derived from the composite of multiple dust proxies—not as a precise
one‑to‑one relationship for each individual proxy. In our analysis, a
one‑standard‑deviation decrease in different dust indicators (station dust frequency,
MISR non‑sphericalAOD, MERRA‑2 dust column mass density) is associated with a
western Indian Ocean warming of roughly 0.5 K. Because each proxy has its own
magnitude of variability, the exact warming per standard deviation slightly differs
across indicators; the value of ~0.5 K represents a central estimate from the
multi‑proxy analysis. We have revised the relevant text in the manuscript to clarify
thispoint and to avoid any potentialmisinterpretation.
The regression coefficients from the multi-proxy analysis collectively suggest that a
decrease in Middle Eastern dust loading is associated with a western Indian Ocean
warming of approximately 0.5 K per standard deviation, a magnitude comparable to
SSTanomalies observed duringmoderate IOD events.
7. Line 336, ‘suppress eastern upwelling’, should that be suppress eastern
downwelling?
Reply:Thank you.Wehave revised as suggested.

Review of “Middle East Dust as a Dominant External Driver of the Indian Ocean
Dipole” by Liu et al.
This study examined how mineral dust aerosols emitted from the Middle East a7ect the
Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) using both observational data and the CESM model. While
previous studies have examined how anthropogenic aerosols e7ect IOD, how Middle
Eastern dust aerosols a7ect the IOD is largely unclear. The study addresses a very
important question in the region, and the topic is very novel and inspiring. The overall
analysis is quite comprehensive, however, some details in model setting, the feedback link
from subtropical dust loading to tropical SSTs, and the magnitude of the radiative forcing
need further clarification. Adding some discussion about the uncertainties in data and
methodology also would strengthen the paper.
Major concerns:
1. Usually, the lifetime of dust aerosols in the atmosphere, especially in the lower
troposphere, is fairly short, from several days to a couple of weeks. The statement
“multi-month atmospheric residence time of dust aerosols” (line 60) needs more
evidence to support. I think it is important to understand whether the strong
connection between JJA Middle Eastern dust and SON IOD is primarily due to an
usually long residence time of summertime Middle Eastern dust, or instead a
delayed response through ocean-atmosphere feedback. It would also be helpful to
clarify whether Middle Eastern dust in SON has any impact on the IOD in SON.
2. The averaging area for the summertime Middle East Dust (SMED) index was not very
clear (e.g., in Fig, 1c). As shown in Figs. 1a and 1b, the domain only covers southern
Middle East, and it also includes the Horn of Africa, which is often not
geographically considered part the Middle East. In the Methods section, there is a
definition of Middle East dust (“10° S–30° N, 35° E–70° E”, line 522). But It’s unclear if
this the averaging region used to calculate all the time series of SMED. And also, the
domain is a quite large, while most of the Middle East dust are located to the north
of 10° N (supplementary Fig. 1). Are the results sensitive to the averaging area of
SMED? Would the correlations change much if only averaging over the region with
high dust loading, e.g., to the north of 10° N?
3. The radiative forcing of the dust aerosols are shown in both the coupled CESM
simulations and atmosphere-only model (CAM) runs. However, the location of
radiative forcing directly from the dust aerosols. With reduced Middle Eastern dust
aerosols , one would expect to see enhanced shortwave (SW) fluxes (i.e., warming)
at the surface extending from the Arabian Peninsula southward toward the Arabian
Sea. However, this pattern is not clearly shown in the coupled simulation (Fig. S8c)--
there is a cooling around 12 °N, while the warming single is located further south,
round 6 °N-6 °S, where the climatological dust loading is low. Is this due to a
teleconnection?
Peninsula towards the Arabian Sea (Figs. S13a, S10a), but mainly over the northern
and eastern Arabian Sea. And the changes in SW flux over the western tropical
Indian Ocean are relatively weak. Does this imply a teleconnection that allow the
local radiative impact of dust aerosols over the Arabian Peninsula and northern
Arabian Sea to propagate to the tropical Indican Ocean?
4. Regarding the mechanisms of dust radiative forcing, it would be more convincing to
include figures to show radiative fluxes at the TOA and also vertical heating profiles
in the regions with high dust loading.
5. Some aspects of the model simulation setup are not very clear. In the CESM
coupled simulation from 1980 to 2020, besides SMED, what other forcings are
included? Are anthropogenic aerosols and greenhouse gases included in the
model? Do they vary over time? What’s the spin-up time for the coupled run?
It is mentioned that dust aerosols are prescribed in the model, however, it is not
clear which dust variable was perturbed. Was it dust AOD, dust mass concentration
at each pressure level, or emission fluxes? And is dust prescribed only the Middle
East (leaving the rest of the world dust-free) or globally? It states that “we drove
CESM with observed summertime dust mass density “(line 523), but it is unclear
which observational dataset was used, and whether the forcing is applied only
during the summer months or throughout the year. Are both dry and wet deposition
included in the model?
6. For the sensitivity test with reduced dust loading, was the forcing applied only in
summertime or all year round? It would be helpful to include a table summarizing
key features of each simulation.
7. It is recommended to include some discussion about the uncertainties of the study.
For instance, in model simulations, dust content is prescribed, so any feedback
from atmospheric circulation to the dust loading is not considered. In terms of
station data, what’s the uncertainty in measurements? Do the station location and
numbers change from 1980 to 2020? Does the uneven spatial distribution of the
stations a7ect the results?
Minor comments:
1. Line 64, it may be helpful to show the response the strongest in SON.
2. Lines 78-79, it is not clear what averaging area is used for the MISR non-spherical
AOD.
3. Line 158, this seems to contradict the statement in lines 134-135. Could you please
clarify what the systematic biases are?
2
4. Line 175, there is also a weak increase in the mixed layer depth over the eastern
tropical Indian Ocean from 100°E to 108 °E (Fig. 2b). What could be the cause of
this?
5. Line 219, regression analysis is less straightforward than performing another
simulation without the variability of Middle Eastern dust and comparing the
di7erences. Conducting a linear regression assumes that the relationships are
linear, which may not necessarily be true.
6. Line 220, “Increased solar radiation penetrates to the surface…” , this is not clearly
shown in Fig. S8c, especially over the region with reduced dust. Please clarify.
7. Lines 221-225, it's not clear why the coupled results are already available (line 192) but
then the analysis switches to an atmosphere-only model, and then returns to the
coupled simulation.
8. Line 229-230 “the direct radiative eMects of reduced dust”, is it possible to clarify the
location of this eMect in the figure?
9. Line 267, the response of shortwave fluxes is mainly over the land. How does the
signal propagate to the TIO?
10. Lines 275-276, “(Extended Data fig. 10)”, isn't the figure from the atmosphere-only
model run (as mentioned in line 221)?
11. Line 304, cooler western part?
12. Line 355, do you mean “reduced dust anomalies”
13. Line 360, dust forcing in JJA or SON?
14. Lines 252-257, how is this done? Are you using the ratio of JJA MERRA-2 dust AOD to
modeled dust AOD to scale dust loading in each month?
15. Line 258, “by perturbing initial temperature fields”, is it land or ocean surface
temperature? How large are the perturbation?s

Summary:
Liu et al. estimated that dust aerosols from the Middle East regions act as a dominant
external driver of the Indian Ocean Dipole. In particular, they show that summertime
dust over the 1980-2020 period accounts for ~36% of interannual IOD variance,
surpassing the El Niño-Southern Oscillation as the main driver during boreal autumn,
using satellite observations and reanalysis. In addition, they perform CSEM v1.2 with
the Parallel Ocean Program (POP2) and Community Atmosphere Model simulations
(CAMS 4.3)toshow that reduced summertimeMiddleEast dust enhances warming in
the western Indian Ocean during boreal autumn and induces easterly winds that shoal
the eastern thermocline. This tilts of the thermocline, deepening it in the west and
shoaling it in the east, and reinforces the SST gradient through the Bjerknes and
wind–evaporation–sea surface temperature (WES) feedback, amplifying a positive
IODpattern, and viceversa.
Overall, the central findings are scientifically interesting and clearly relevant to Indian
Ocean climate variability, particularly the assessment that summertime Middle East
dust explains a large fraction of IOD interannual variance, potentially surpassing
ENSO’s influence during boreal autumn. However, characterizing Middle Eastern
dust aerosols as thedominant external driver of IOD variability is currently overstated.
Amore explicit differentiation between the impacts of Middle Eastern dust and those
of Central and East Asian dust emissions is required, as both may modulate the IOD.
Furthermore, additional forcings and modes of variability, including anthropogenic
aerosols, greenhouse gases, the Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO), and the Pacific
Decadal Oscillation (PDO), can also affect IOD variability during boreal autumn.
These contributions should be carefully separated and quantified before making the
strong claim that MiddleEast dust isthedominant external driver oftheIOD.

This study examined how mineral dust aerosols emitted from the Middle East a7ect
the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) using both observational data and the CESM model.
While previous studies have examined how anthropogenic aerosols effect IOD, how
Middle Eastern dust aerosols affect the IOD is largely unclear. The study addresses a
very important question in the region, and the topic is very novel and inspiring. The
overall analysis is quite comprehensive, however, some details in model setting, the
feedback link from subtropical dust loading totropical SSTs, and the magnitude ofthe
radiative forcing need further clarification. Adding some discussion about the
uncertainties indata and methodology also would strengthen thepaper.

original comments are shown in blue. Our replies are shown in black. The
corresponding changes in themanuscript are shown in Italicblack.

1. Usually, the lifetime of dust aerosols in the atmosphere, especially in the lower
troposphere, is fairly short, from several days to a couple of weeks. The statement
“multi-month atmospheric residence time of dust aerosols” (line 60) needs more
evidence to support. I think it is important to understand whether the strong
connection between JJA Middle Eastern dust and SON IOD is primarily due to an
usually long residence time of summertime Middle Eastern dust, or instead a delayed

Reply:Thank you foryour valuablecomments and insightful suggestions.
We agree that the near-surface residence time of dust aerosols is relatively short. The
original statement referring to a "multi-month atmospheric residence time" has been
revised for greater precision, and supporting references have been added. The revised
text now emphasizes that under specific conditions—such as when dust is lifted by
strong upward air currents into the stratosphere or when fine-grained particles
undergo long-range transport—certain fractions of dust aerosols may exhibit extended
residence times (e.g., exceeding one month). We have cited relevant studies on
transatlantic transport of Saharan dust and trans-Pacific transport of Asian dust (Kim
et al., 2019; Prospero et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2019a; Yu et al., 2019b), illustrating that
under favorable atmospheric circulation conditions, fine dust particles can remain in
theatmosphere from several weeks tomonths.
Moreover, your distinction between the two possible mechanisms—long residence
time versus delayed ocean–atmosphere feedback—is indeed critical. The
ocean–atmosphere interaction is likely the dominant mechanism. Specifically, Middle
Eastern dust in summer may influence the radiative balance and thus affect sea
surface temperature patterns over the Arabian Sea and western Indian Ocean by the
delayed response through ocean-atmosphere feedback. These effects may
subsequently trigger an IOD event in the following season through air–sea
interactions.
Additionally, Middle Eastern dust in SON has limited direct influence on the IOD
during the same season as validated by various dust proxies (Fig. R1). This may be
attributed to the generally weaker dust activity in the Middle East during autumn
(Extended Data Fig. 1c in the revised manuscript), as well as the fact that the IOD is
already in its mature phase by SON, during which coupled ocean–atmosphere
processes dominate its evolution and external forcings such as dust play a relatively
minorrole.

3. The radiative forcing of the dust aerosols are shown in both the coupled CESM
simulations and atmosphere-only model (CAM) runs. However, the location of
radiative forcing directly from the dust aerosols. With reduced Middle Eastern dust
aerosols , one would expect to see enhanced shortwave (SW) fluxes (i.e., warming)
at the surface extending from theArabian Peninsula southward toward theArabian Sea.
However, this pattern is not clearly shown in the coupled simulation (Fig. S8c)--there

Reply: Thank you for this insightful observation regarding the spatial pattern of
surface shortwave radiation response in our coupled model experiments. You have
correctly identified a key nuance in how dust aerosol impacts manifest in coupled
versus atmosphere-only simulations.
You rightly noted that reduced Middle Eastern dust should directly enhance surface
shortwave fluxes over dust-laden regions from the Arabian Peninsula to the Arabian
Sea. This expected response is clearly present in our atmosphere-only (CAM)
experiments, as shown in Extended Data Fig. 14a.The different pattern in the coupled
(CESM) simulation—with cooling near 12°N and warming displaced farther
south—is indeed attributable to ocean-atmosphere coupling and the associated
teleconnections as you suggested. The initial radiative perturbation triggers a specific
chain of adjustments:
(1) Circulation Adjustment: The surface warming over the western Tropical Indian
Ocean (TIO) enhances convection and establishes a low-pressure anomaly (Fig. 2c).
This sets up a basin-scale pressure gradient, driving an anomalous clockwise vertical
circulation and generating prevailing anomalous easterly winds at the surface over the
centralTIO, oppositetotheclimatological westerlies (Fig. 2c-d).
(2) Mechanism for the Displaced Warming: These easterly anomalies suppress the
eastward advection of warm water and, through Bjerknes and wind-evaporation-SST
(WES) feedbacks, help sustain and confine the core of the warming signal further
south, near 6°N–6°S.
(3) Mechanism for the Cooling near 12°N: Crucially, in the region near 12°N
(Arabian Sea), the circulation adjustment leads to a strengthening of the prevailing
climatological winds (Fig. 2c, vectors). This increase in surface wind speed enhances
local evaporation, which produces a net surface cooling via the WES feedback. This
wind-driven cooling effectively counteracts and overshadows the direct radiative
warming from dust reduction, resulting in the net cooling anomaly observed in
Extended Data Fig. 14c.
In summary, the coupling-induced atmospheric circulation adjustment—particularly
the wind speed changes and the subsequent WES feedback—redistributes the thermal
response, explaining both the southward shift of the warming and the localized
cooling around 12°N.
Therefore, we have expanded the discussion in the revised manuscript to explicitly
address thismechanism.Wealso cited thediscussion here for convenience.
Moreover, the atmospheric-only simulation exhibits a radiative response that is
spatially coherent with the dust aerosol distribution (Extended Data Fig. 14), while
the coupled simulation displays additional spatial heterogeneity due to oceanic
adjustments (Extended Data Fig. 11). This redistribution likely stems from
ocean-atmosphere coupling, wherein the initial radiative perturbation triggers
atmospheric circulation adjustments andsubsequent wind-evaporation-SSTfeedbacks,
creating secondary radiative perturbations that partially obscure the direct
dust–radiation signal, which is ultimately manifested as a teleconnected response.
Nevertheless, both experiments consistently support the proposed physical framework
linkingMiddle Eastern dust forcing to IODvariability.
4. In the CAM simulations, enhanced SW fluxes do appear from southern Arabian
Peninsula towards the Arabian Sea (Figs. S13a, S10a), but mainly over the northern
and easternArabian Sea.And the changes in SW flux over the western tropical Indian
Ocean are relatively weak. Does this imply a teleconnection that allow the local
radiative impact of dust aerosols over theArabian Peninsulaand northernArabian Sea
topropagate to thetropical Indian Ocean?
Reply: Thank you for this perceptive question, which gets to the heart of the
dynamical mechanisms at play. You are correct in observing that the enhanced SW
fluxes in the CAM simulations are concentrated over the northern and easternArabian
Sea, with a weaker direct signal over the western tropical Indian Ocean. This spatial
structure indeed implies that the local radiative forcing from reduced dust does not
remain confined, but rather initiates an atmospheric teleconnection that propagates its
influence downstream.
Themechanism isa three-step process:
(1) Local Radiative Forcing & Atmospheric Adjustment: Reduced dust over the
Arabian Peninsula/northern Arabian Sea increases surface SW absorption, creating a
strong vertical heating gradient (surface warming, relative upper-level cooling;
Extended Data Figs.11, 13a).Thismodifies local stabilityand circulation.
(2) Atmospheric Teleconnection & Downstream Cloud Response: The adjusted
circulation and zonal cell (Fig. 2d) act as a teleconnection bridge, transporting the
perturbation's influence to the western TIO. This alters the vertical thermodynamic
profile, driving a characteristic cloud reorganization there: decreased low-level and
increased high-level cloud cover (Fig. 3c, d). In the atmosphere-only (CAM) run, this
teleconnected response is limited by fixed SSTs, explaining the weaker direct
maritimesignal.
(3) Amplification via Ocean-Atmosphere Coupling: This step explains the stronger
oceanic signal in the coupled model. The teleconnected cloud changes (Step 2) now
interact with the ocean. Reduced low cloud cover increases surface shortwave
radiation, leading to SST warming. This warming then activates powerful positive
feedback loops: the cloud–SST feedback further suppressing low clouds (Lin et al.,
2025; Wu et al., 2025; Wyant et al., 1997), the Bjerknes feedback and the
wind‑evaporation‑SST (WES) feedback. These coupled feedbacks dramatically
amplify and extend theinitial atmospheric perturbation.
Therefore, the CAM pattern confirms the dust reduction initiates an atmospheric
teleconnection. The coupling with the ocean is essential to transform this initial
adjustment into the stronger, basin-scale ocean-atmosphere feedbacks that effectively
drive the IOD development, as detailed in our manuscript. We have expanded the
discussion in the revised manuscript to explicitly address this mechanism. We also
cited thediscussion here for convenience.
Notably, the spatial pattern of the SW flux response in the CAM simulations, with its
maximum over the northern and eastern Arabian Sea rather than uniformly across the
basin (Extended Data Fig. 17a &c), suggests that the radiative impact of dust
reduction initiates an atmospheric teleconnection. The initial perturbation mainly
over the land likely alters regional atmospheric heating and circulation patterns 46-48,
which in turn redistributes the energy downstream, setting the stage for the more
extensive and evident ocean-atmosphere signals and feedbacks that propagating to
theTIOin thecoupled model.

18.Line 267, the response of shortwave fluxes is mainly over the land. How does the
signal propagate to theTIO?
Reply: Thank you for raising this question.The signal propagates from the land tothe
Tropical Indian Ocean (TIO) primarily through an atmospheric teleconnection. The
mechanism is athree-step process:
(1) Local Radiative Forcing & Atmospheric Adjustment: Reduced dust over the
Arabian Peninsula/northern Arabian Sea increases surface SW absorption, creating a
strong vertical heating gradient (surface warming, relative upper-level cooling;
Extended Data Figs.11, 13a).Thismodifies local stabilityand circulation.
(2) Atmospheric Teleconnection & Downstream Cloud Response: The adjusted
circulation and zonal cell (Fig. 2d) act as a teleconnection bridge, transporting the
perturbation's influence to the western TIO. This alters the vertical thermodynamic
profile, driving a characteristic cloud reorganization there: decreased low-level and
increased high-level cloud cover (Fig. 3c, d). In the atmosphere-only (CAM) run, this
teleconnected response is limited by fixed SSTs, explaining the weaker direct
maritimesignal.
(3) Amplification via Ocean-Atmosphere Coupling: This step explains the stronger
oceanic signal in the coupled model. The teleconnected cloud changes (Step 2) now
interact with the ocean. Reduced low clouds enhance surface SW, warming the SST.
This warming then triggers powerful positive feedbacks: the cloud–SST feedback
further suppressing low clouds (Lin et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Wyant et al., 1997),
the Bjerknes feedbacks and wind-evaporation-SST (WES) feedbacks. These coupled
feedbacks dramatically amplify and extend theinitial atmosphericperturbation.
Therefore, the CAM pattern confirms the dust reduction initiates an atmospheric
teleconnection. The coupling with the ocean is essential to transform this initial
adjustment into the stronger, basin-scale ocean-atmosphere feedbacks that effectively
drivetheIOD development, as detailed inourmanuscript.
In summary, the dust-induced radiative heating over the Middle East perturbs the
regional atmospheric circulation, which in turn triggers a remote response that
influences theTIO.
We have systematically elaborated this dynamical pathway in the revised manuscript
within the " Mechanism: how dust shapes the IOD" section, detailing the key
processes of (1) local radiative adjustment, (2) atmospheric bridge via zonal cell
circulation, and (3) amplification through air-sea feedbacks, and we refer the reader to
that discussionhere.
We have also clarified this dynamical pathway in the revised manuscript and cited it
here.
The initial perturbation mainly over the land likely alters regional atmospheric
heating and circulation patterns 46-48, which in turn redistributes the energy
downstream, setting the stage for the more extensive and evident ocean-atmosphere
signalsandfeedbacks that propagating to theTIOinthe coupled model.

## Abstract

The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) strongly influences Indo-Pacific climate extremes, yet its drivers remain incompletely understood. Using satellite observations, reanalysis, and climate model experiments, we identify Middle East dust emissions as a major external driver of IOD variability. Observational evidence shows that dust over the 1980-2020 period account for ~36% of interannual IOD variance, surpassing El Niño-Southern Oscillation as the main driver during boreal autumn. Climate simulations confirm that reduced dust enhances warming in the western Indian Ocean and induce easterly winds that shoal the eastern thermocline. These anomalies trigger Bjerknes and wind–evaporation–sea surface temperature feedbacks, amplifying a positive IOD pattern, and vice versa. Our findings reveal a powerful dust–IOD teleconnection, highlighting the need to incorporate aerosol forcing into seasonal forecasts and climate projections.

---

## Introduction

The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) is the major mode of interannual climate variability in the Tropical Indian Ocean (TIO), marked by a seesaw pattern of sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies between the western and eastern TIO1,2. This anomalous SST pattern leads to changes in atmospheric circulation and rainfall patterns over the vast areas surrounding TIO, including Indonesia, India, Australia, and East Africa3–5. Positive IOD (pIOD) events bring warming to the western basin and cooling to the east, reshaping rainfall patterns across East Africa, India, Indonesia, and Australia, while negative phases (nIOD) have opposite effects. The extreme pIOD event in 2019 triggered unprecedented Australian bushfires and historic flooding along the Yangtze River6–8, underscoring the urgent need to understand the mechanism underlying IOD events. Most studies attribute IOD variability to external forcing4,9, internal air–sea interactions and remote El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) influences1,10,11, yet the role of aerosols remains largely unexplored. The TIO is located close to the world’s second largest dust source—the Middle East deserts. Previous studies have identified the far-reaching impacts of Middle East dust on the South Asian monsoon, Arabian Sea SST, and Indian summer monsoon rainfall12–14. Around 2010, both IOD behavior and Middle East dust emissions shifted markedly, with IOD transitioning from frequent negative to positive phases and Middle East dust emissions reaching historically low levels by 201915–18. This coincidence motivates our investigation into whether dust forcing influences IOD phases and quantifies its contribution to the variability of IOD.

Here, we show that variability in summertime Middle East dust (SMED) is a critical driver of autumn IOD events. Using model experiments, we establish a causal link where reduced SMED triggers a chain of atmosphere-ocean interactions in the tropical Indian Ocean. These interactions, primarily driven by wind-induced ocean dynamics and reinforced by cloud feedbacks, robustly promote the development of positive IOD conditions.

### Reviewer 1

Liu et al. estimated that dust aerosols from the Middle East regions act as a dominant external driver of the Indian Ocean Dipole. In particular, they show that summertime dust over the 1980-2020 period accounts for ~36% of interannual IOD variance, surpassing the El Niño-Southern Oscillation as the main driver during boreal autumn, using satellite observations and reanalysis. In addition, they perform CSEM v1.2 with the Parallel Ocean Program (POP2) and Community Atmosphere Model simulations (CAMS 4.3) to show that reduced summertime Middle East dust enhances warming in the western Indian Ocean during boreal autumn and induces easterly winds that shoal the eastern thermocline. This tilts of the thermocline, deepening it in the west and shoaling it in the east, and reinforces the SST gradient through the Bjerknes and wind–evaporation–sea surface temperature (WES) feedback, amplifying a positive IOD pattern, and vice versa.
Overall, the central findings are scientifically interesting and clearly relevant to Indian Ocean climate variability, particularly the assessment that summertime Middle East dust explains a large fraction of IOD interannual variance, potentially surpassing ENSO’s influence during boreal autumn. However, characterizing Middle Eastern dust aerosols as the dominant external driver of IOD variability is currently overstated. A more explicit differentiation between the impacts of Middle Eastern dust and those of Central and East Asian dust emissions is required, as both may modulate the IOD. Furthermore, additional forcings and modes of variability, including anthropogenic aerosols, greenhouse gases, the Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO), and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), can also affect IOD variability during boreal autumn. These contributions should be carefully separated and quantified before making the strong claim that Middle East dust is the dominant external driver of the IOD.
Dust variability can both drive and respond to IOD variability. However, this bidirectional relationship does not yet appear to be well constrained in the authors’ analysis of dust–IOD interactions, partly because of substantial uncertainty in the representation of dust emissions in the global climate model CESM v1.2 (Kok et al., 2022; main text reference 18). Given this known bias, the authors should more clearly justify their choice of CESM v1.2 with CAMS 4.3 for this study and explain how this underestimate might affect their conclusions regarding dust–IOD interactions.
Prior work has linked anthropogenic aerosols and greenhouse gases to Indian Ocean warming and IOD-like patterns, and has also shown that Middle East and West Asian dust influences the South Asian monsoon and Arabian Sea SST (see Banerjee and Kumar, 2016; Jin et al., 2014; Zheng and Hoteit, 2025). Also, It has been shown that Indian summer monsoon rainfall responds positively to Middle East dust (Jin and Yang, 2014). These findings from previous studies should be discussed explicitly in the main manuscript.

reduced low-level clouds (e.g., stratocumulus), which decreases planetary albedo.
Conversely, the increase in longwave radiation is linked to enhanced high-level cloud

This explanation is now grounded in established cloud-radiative feedback theory,

The transformation of cloud fields—characterized by a reduction in low-level cloud
fraction and an increase in high-level cloud fraction—further modifies the radiative
budget (Figs. 3a, b). Specifically, the decrease in low clouds reduces the albedo,
allowing more shortwave radiation to penetrate and warm the ocean surface 37,38.

by absorbing and re-emitting longwave radiation, which inhibits radiative cooling at
the surface 37,39. These two effects act in synergy with the direct radiative effect of
reduced dust loading to amplify the warming signal over the western TIO. This cloud
feedback process, particularly the low-cloud albedo feedback, is well-established as a
key positivefeedback mechanism modulating TIOvariability.

Summary:
This study examined how mineral dust aerosols emitted from the Middle East a7ect
the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) using both observational data and the CESM model.
While previous studies have examined how anthropogenic aerosols effect IOD, how
Middle Eastern dust aerosols affect the IOD is largely unclear. The study addresses a
very important question in the region, and the topic is very novel and inspiring. The
overall analysis is quite comprehensive, however, some details in model setting, the
feedback link from subtropical dust loading totropical SSTs, and the magnitude ofthe
radiative forcing need further clarification. Adding some discussion about the
uncertainties indata and methodology also would strengthen thepaper.
Reply: We are grateful to the reviewer for his/her insightful and very valuable
suggestions, which have significantly contributed to the enhancement of our
manuscript. We have carefully addressed the comments and made the necessary
revisions, hoping that the updated version meets the journal's standards. Our
responses to each of the comments and suggestions are as follows. The referee’s
original comments are shown in blue. Our replies are shown in black. The
corresponding changes in themanuscript are shown in Italicblack.
Majorcomments
1. Usually, the lifetime of dust aerosols in the atmosphere, especially in the lower
troposphere, is fairly short, from several days to a couple of weeks. The statement
“multi-month atmospheric residence time of dust aerosols” (line 60) needs more
evidence to support. I think it is important to understand whether the strong
connection between JJA Middle Eastern dust and SON IOD is primarily due to an
usually long residence time of summertime Middle Eastern dust, or instead a delayed
response through ocean-atmosphere feedback. It would also be helpful to clarify
whether MiddleEastern dust in SONhas any impact ontheIOD inSON.
Reply:Thank you foryour valuablecomments and insightful suggestions.
We agree that the near-surface residence time of dust aerosols is relatively short. The
original statement referring to a "multi-month atmospheric residence time" has been
revised for greater precision, and supporting references have been added. The revised
text now emphasizes that under specific conditions—such as when dust is lifted by
strong upward air currents into the stratosphere or when fine-grained particles
undergo long-range transport—certain fractions of dust aerosols may exhibit extended
residence times (e.g., exceeding one month). We have cited relevant studies on
transatlantic transport of Saharan dust and trans-Pacific transport of Asian dust (Kim
et al., 2019; Prospero et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2019a; Yu et al., 2019b), illustrating that
under favorable atmospheric circulation conditions, fine dust particles can remain in
theatmosphere from several weeks tomonths.
Moreover, your distinction between the two possible mechanisms—long residence
time versus delayed ocean–atmosphere feedback—is indeed critical. The
ocean–atmosphere interaction is likely the dominant mechanism. Specifically, Middle
Eastern dust in summer may influence the radiative balance and thus affect sea
surface temperature patterns over the Arabian Sea and western Indian Ocean by the
delayed response through ocean-atmosphere feedback. These effects may
subsequently trigger an IOD event in the following season through air–sea
interactions.
Additionally, Middle Eastern dust in SON has limited direct influence on the IOD
during the same season as validated by various dust proxies (Fig. R1). This may be
attributed to the generally weaker dust activity in the Middle East during autumn
(Extended Data Fig. 1c in the revised manuscript), as well as the fact that the IOD is
already in its mature phase by SON, during which coupled ocean–atmosphere
processes dominate its evolution and external forcings such as dust play a relatively
minorrole.

3. The radiative forcing of the dust aerosols are shown in both the coupled CESM
simulations and atmosphere-only model (CAM) runs. However, the location of
radiative forcing directly from the dust aerosols. With reduced Middle Eastern dust
aerosols, one would expect to see enhanced shortwave (SW) fluxes (i.e., warming)
at the surface extending from theArabian Peninsula southward toward theArabian Sea.
However, this pattern is not clearly shown in the coupled simulation (Fig. S8c)--there
is a cooling around 12 °N, while the warming single is located further south, round
